meta.title: The G Form: Three Roots, All Six Strings
meta.summary: The G form carries three roots across all six strings, which makes it the best form for seeing where a chord lives and the hardest to hold whole.

. That window holds three roots, not two — the first form in this chapter with more than a pair. Both the C form and the A form only gave you two roots each; here the count changes, and so does what the form is good for.
. Low, middle, and high — the G form is the only one of the five that touches the bottom of the neck, the middle, and the top at once.

props.caption: Three roots: string 6 fret 8, string 3 fret 5, string 1 fret 8

spans.text: Strings 6 and 1 are tuned exactly two octaves apart, so any note on the low E has a twin on the high e at the very same fret. Here both roots land on

. It is the cheapest fact on the fretboard, and the G form is where it is impossible to miss — the two outer strings of the window, same fret, same letter. It is also the one octave relationship on the whole neck that needs no arithmetic: find a note on string 6 anywhere, in any key, and you have already found it on string 1, at the same fret, for free.
String 6 and string 1, same fret, always the same note two octaves apart. The G form just happens to put both roots in view together.
, is already familiar — it was the A form's upper root. One note, claimed by two forms, and it won't be the last time that happens.

Three roots is not trivia here — it is what the form is for. With a root on the bottom string, the middle string, and the top string, you can start a phrase at the bottom of the neck, in the middle of it, or right up near the top, all without leaving this one window. The C and A forms only told you about the bottom half; the G form's three roots span the whole thing, and that is what makes it the best form for simply seeing where a chord lives.
Character-wise, that width is also the catch. The G form is the

of the five and the hardest to hold whole. A barre at fret 5 while the outer fingers reach up to fret 8 is a stretch most hands decline, so in practice this form gets played in pieces — and each piece is for something specific. The top three strings give you a root on string 1 with the rest of the chord sitting right under it, useful wherever a lead line is already living up there. The low root paired with the string 3 root gives you the chord's two lowest anchors, useful for holding down the bottom of a progression without the stretch. That is the same fragment habit the C form introduced, not a new idea: wide forms get played partially, as the normal case, and which piece you take depends on what you need it for.
